clue.text: Have little hope of putting the squeeze on some suckers?

definitions.text: Have little hope of putting the squeeze on some suckers?

parts.words: Have little hope of putting the squeeze on some suckers?
parts.note: drinking straws are suckers, and gripping them hard is a picture of the desperate grab made by someone with almost no hope left

explanation.surface: Someone doubts their chances of squeezing money out of gullible people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suckers' reads as dupes being squeezed for cash; here it means drinking straws, which are sucked, and the idiom is a last desperate grab.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a desperate person seizing any slim chance, which is what someone with little hope does.

clue.text: Stay temporarily with some masons

definitions.meaning: to stay as a ... in someone's house for a time
a branch of Freemasons forms a local group with its own meeting hall

explanation.surface: Someone stays briefly with a few Freemasons.
explanation.definitionFit: To board somewhere for a short while is one sense; a local branch of Freemasons meeting together is the other.

clue.text: Formal agreement to attempt to dine in

indicators.note: in says the dining word goes inside the attempt word

parts.note: an attempt is a try
to dine is to eat

explanation.surface: A formal pact to try having dinner together.
explanation.definitionFit: A pact signed between states is a formal agreement, the standard dictionary sense.

clue.text: Cheer pilot going off in this?

definitions.text: Cheer pilot going off in this?

indicators.note: going off suggests something exploding or departing, so the letters of the two words are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A cheerful aviator takes off in this machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going off' turns CHEER PILOT into the craft itself, and the whole clue also describes a pilot flying off in one.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotor-driven aircraft is what a pilot would take off in, the whole clue painting the scene.

clue.text: Won't move to urban area

indicators.note: move tells us to shift the letters of the word around into another order

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to relocate to the city.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Won't' is ignored, leaving four letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A built-up settlement larger than a village is an urban area.

clue.text: Row of houses where artist joined in monastic service

indicators.note: joined in pictures the artist taking part inside the service, so those letters go inside

parts.note: terce is the monastic office said at the third hour of the day
RA stands for Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist

explanation.surface: A street where a painter took part in the monks' worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joined in' reads as the artist taking part in worship; terce is the office monks say at the third hour, about 9 a.m.
explanation.definitionFit: A line of joined houses built in a continuous block is a common British housing form.

clue.text: A daughter doing woodwork? Touching

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter in family trees
joinery is woodworking, so a carpenter at work is joining

explanation.surface: A girl takes up carpentry, which is touching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touching' looks like praise for the scene, but it means next to or in contact.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things side by side with a shared edge are in contact, the adjective sense.

clue.text: Teacher in college married, I emphasise

parts.note: a college can be called a school
to emphasise is to stress

explanation.surface: A college teacher insists she is married.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who teaches pupils was traditionally given this title, an old-fashioned word for a female teacher.

clue.text: Its members have no peer

parts.note: the elected MPs of the lower chamber of Parliament are not peers, who sit in the Lords instead; the surface reads as praise for unequalled members

explanation.surface: A club whose members are without equal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like 'equal'; it means a member of the House of Lords, the other chamber of the UK Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Parliament in the elected chamber are commoners, not peers of the realm.

clue.text: Chap who's not even a charitable type

definitions.meaning: a man who is odd, as an odd number is not even
a British friendly society, a benevolent mutual-aid group

explanation.surface: A man who is odd-numbered turns out to be a benevolent sort.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oddfellows are a long-standing British friendly society whose members help one another.
explanation.definitionFit: An odd man is a strange chap; a member of the Oddfellows friendly society is a mutual-aid charity member.

clue.text: Prince gives a little open backing to hospital

indicators.note: backing means the word for slightly open is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: a door slightly open is ajar

explanation.surface: A prince gives some support to an open hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' looks like support for the hospital but turns AJAR into RAJA.
explanation.definitionFit: An Indian king or ruler holds this title, so it can stand for a prince.

clue.text: One who doubts being infected, having caught cold

indicators.note: having caught pictures the infected word catching the cold inside it

parts.note: an infected wound is septic
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A doubter is worried about infection after catching a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught cold' reads as an illness, but C for cold goes inside SEPTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A doubter who questions accepted claims is the plain dictionary sense.

clue.text: Alice shortly to enter firm making cloth

indicators.note: to enter puts the shortened name inside the firm

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm

indicators.note: shortly tells us to cut the name short, dropping its final letter

explanation.surface: Alice is soon to join a company making fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' looks like 'soon' but trims Alice to ALI, which goes into CO.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain-woven cotton fabric, often printed, is a kind of cloth.

clue.text: Exclusive alternatives? Not exactly

definitions.meaning: two options that cannot both hold, a greater amount or a smaller one

explanation.surface: Mutually exclusive options, or not quite.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally the phrase offers two opposite options; as an idiom it means roughly or approximately.

clue.text: Acknowledging mistake, starting to write next answer backwards

indicators.note: backwards says the kept opening is then read in reverse
starting to write means only the opening part of that answer is kept

parts.note: the next across answer in the grid is the clue at 17

explanation.surface: Someone admits an error as they begin writing the following answer back to front.
explanation.walkthrough: The next answer is 17 Across; its first four letters, SPOO, read backwards give the exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is what people blurt when owning up to a small blunder.

clue.text: Fasten badge of rank on jacket material

parts.note: to fasten something is to pin it
a stripe on a sleeve shows military rank

explanation.surface: Pin a rank insignia onto a jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is only a link joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth with thin parallel lines is the classic fabric for business suits and jackets.

clue.text: Often amusing confusion of speech after initial exchange

definitions.text: Often amusing confusion of speech after initial exchange

parts.words: Often amusing confusion of speech after initial exchange
parts.note: a slip in which the opening sounds of two words swap places, usually producing a comic phrase

explanation.surface: A funny verbal muddle following a first conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initial exchange' looks like a first chat; it means the first letters of words being swapped, named after the Reverend Spooner.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip of the tongue that transposes the starting sounds of words is a comic verbal mix-up.

clue.text: Clean rivet may fail in such a bridge

indicators.note: may fail suggests the parts coming apart, so these letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A clean rivet could give way in this kind of bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such a bridge' points back at the whole clue for the type of bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge built from beams projecting out from piers and supported at one end is a well-known engineering type.

clue.text: Troublemaker everyone wanted to arraign

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous troublemaker
each means every one

explanation.surface: A mischief-maker that everybody wanted to put on trial.
explanation.definitionFit: To formally accuse a public official of wrongdoing is to charge them before a tribunal.

clue.text: What's laid for breakfast

parts.note: a table is laid for a meal, but hens lay the morning food itself

explanation.surface: The things set out for the morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid' suggests setting the table; it is what hens do.
explanation.definitionFit: Hens produce these, and they are a standard morning food.

clue.text: Come down with gold coach

parts.note: to come down from the air is to land
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: Descend with a golden carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a folding hood is a kind of coach.

clue.text: Feature of classical architecture — some came to Persia

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Elements of ancient Greek building styles travelled to Persia.
explanation.definitionFit: A square panel between triglyphs in a Doric frieze is a classical building element.

clue.text: Clergyman touring a power plant

indicators.note: touring pictures the clergyman going around the letter, so it sits inside

parts.note: a rector is a parish clergyman

explanation.surface: A vicar shows visitors around an electricity station.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuclear installation that generates energy from fission is a kind of power station.

clue.text: People securing ranks

definitions.meaning: those who tie things up to secure them
rows or levels arranged one above another

explanation.surface: Those who fasten things, or rows.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who tie knots are fastening people; stacked rows of seats or levels are ranks.

clue.text: Show disapproval of king being rough, rude type

parts.note: to boo is to jeer in disapproval
R is the abbreviation for king, from the Latin rex

explanation.surface: Jeering at a monarch for being an uncouth lout.
explanation.definitionFit: An ill-mannered, coarse person is a lout or oaf.

clue.text: Board approval from Paris and Berlin

parts.note: oui is French for yes
ja is German for yes, the approval carried over to Berlin

explanation.surface: A committee gets endorsement from France and Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' looks like a committee; it is the lettered board used at séances, named from French and German yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A lettered séance tablet with a pointer is a talking board, named from two words for yes.

clue.text: Get excessively clobbered

parts.note: clobber is British slang for clothes, so being clobbered too much means wearing too many fine clothes, not being beaten up

explanation.surface: Someone takes a severe beating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clobbered' suggests a hammering; in British slang clobber means clothing or gear.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear clothes too formal or elaborate for an occasion is to put on too much finery.

clue.text: Plant countryman puts his money in?

definitions.meaning: a wild flowering weed of the mustard family
a rural herdsman's bag for coins, read literally

explanation.surface: A plant where a rural man stores his cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A common weed with heart-shaped seed pods is one sense; a flock-keeper's wallet is the playful literal reading.
